books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, A. The Second Two-Party System: The Democrats and the Whigs
The Whig Party and the Second Party System

stimulus.text:
| | Democrats | Whigs |
|---|---|---|
| Leading figure | Andrew Jackson | Henry Clay |
| Federal government | Limited; opposed a national bank, high tariffs, and internal improvements | Active; favored a national bank, tariffs, and internal improvements |
| Main supporters | Southern planters, western farmers, and urban immigrants | Northern manufacturers, commercial interests, and evangelical Protestants |

stem: A voter who favored Henry Clay's American System would most likely have supported which candidate in the election of 1832?

options.misconception: Jackson won the election, so it is easy to think every program's supporters voted for him.
Van Buren was a famous Democrat, so it is easy to attach any Democratic-era program to him.
Calhoun was Jackson's great rival, so it is easy to cast him as the opposition candidate.

rationales.A: Jackson vetoed the Bank's recharter and opposed the American System; its supporters voted against him.
rationales.B: Clay designed the American System, a national bank, tariffs, and internal improvements, and he ran against Jackson in 1832 on that program.
rationales.C: Van Buren was Jackson's ally and successor, not the champion of Clay's program.
rationales.D: Calhoun had been Jackson's vice president and led the nullifiers; he did not run as the American System's candidate in 1832.
rationales.general:
1. Match the program to the man. The American System was Henry Clay's plan: a bank, tariffs, and improvements.
2. Match the man to the ballot. Clay ran for president in 1832 against Jackson, making the Bank the campaign's central issue.
Background: Jackson vetoed the recharter, Van Buren backed Jackson, and Calhoun led the other opposition.
Remember: a program's name is a clue to its author — follow the name to the candidate.
